title: Glacier surges on James Ross Island, Antarctica, and their relationship with climate
abstract: Abstract. Although the Antarctic Peninsula has a similar climate to that of other regions hosting surge-type glaciers, only one glacier surge has been previously observed in this region. We examined ice surface velocity, elevation and terminus position changes of Antarctic Peninsula glaciers to identify glacier surges. This revealed only four surges from three glaciers, all on James Ross Island. Gourdon Glacier surged from 2005 to 2007 then again from 2013 to 2018, Kotick Glacier surged during 2013 to 2017 and Whisky Glacier surged from 2020 to 2024. All four surges were characterised by significant advances in glacier terminus position and, for the latter three surges where observations are more abundant, at least an order-of-magnitude speed-up and mass transfer from upper to lower parts of each glacier. The landform record and historical imagery suggest additional surges of Kotick Glacier and Gourdon Glacier may have occurred in the second half of the 20th century. Reanalyses, reconstructions and observations of air temperature suggest that atmospheric warming since 1940 has increasingly exposed these and neighbouring glaciers on the northern tip of the Antarctic Peninsula and its surrounding islands to conditions that are typical of surge-type glaciers globally. Climate projections indicate that future warming will expose more glaciers on the Peninsula to climatic conditions conducive to surging until the mid-20th century, after which the surge-conducive area remains steady under Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) 2-4.5 and declines under SSP5-8.5. This suggests that surges on the Antarctic Peninsula may become more common over the coming decades, motivating continued monitoring.
problem: The paper addresses the discrepancy that, despite the Antarctic Peninsula having a climate suitable for surge-type glaciers, only one such surge had been previously observed, indicating a significant gap in understanding the region's glaciological behavior.
method: This study identifies and characterizes glacier surges on James Ross Island by examining changes in ice surface velocity, elevation, and terminus position from satellite and historical imagery, and places these observations within the context of past and future climate models.
task: The task is to identify and characterize recent glacier surges on James Ross Island, Antarctica, using satellite observations and historical records, and to investigate their relationship with past and future climate change.
innovation: This paper documents four glacier surges from three glaciers on James Ross Island, Antarctica, between 2005 and 2024, significantly expanding the observational record and linking their occurrence to regional climate warming that creates conditions conducive to surging.

Gourdon Glacier underwent a phase of acceleration, ice surface elevation change and terminus position change between 2013 and 2020. Ice surface speed increased between 2013 and 2016, reaching peak speeds of 325 m yr¯¹ in 2015 (13 times the average speed during 2000 to 2005), before speeds returned to ~25 m yr¹ by 2020 (Figure 4k). We note that our velocity data do not capture the beginning of this acceleration – speeds were already four times greater in 2013 than those observed in 2000. Clear summertime speed-ups in 2014/2015 and 2015/2016 were superimposed on the period of elevated speeds. Interestingly, flow speed decreased in a step-wise manner, interrupted by periods of a few months to over a year in which flow speed was relatively constant. From 2015 to 2017, Gourdon Glacier thinned by 2.4 m in its upper reaches (blue line in Figure 4i) whilst the central and lower portions of the tongue thickened by almost five metres (black and magenta lines in Figure 4i). Thinning of the entire glacier occurred from 2017 to 2023, with thinning of up to ten metres in the lowest part of the glacier. Since March 2023, the upper reaches of the glacier have been thickening by 2.7 m yr¹ and, if those rates continue, the glacier will regain its pre-surge ice thickness in September 2029 (Figure 4i, Supplementary Figure 3). The terminus advanced by 180 m from March 2015 to January 2018, before retreating through to 2025 (Figure 4m).
